point: Corrects the premise: the asker does not have to enroll in Part B this month. Someone 65+ covered by a group health plan based on their own or a spouse's current employment has a Part B Special Enrollment Period: they can sign up in any month while still working and covered, or in the 8 months beginning the month after the job or the coverage ends (whichever ends first), with no late-enrollment penalty (42 U.S.C. 1395p(i)). The coworker's lifetime penalty (10% per full 12 months without Part B) applies only when there is no SEP.

With about 400 employees (20 or more), the employer plan pays first and Medicare pays second (42 U.S.C. 1395y(b)(1)(A)), so taking Part B now only buys secondary coverage at the 2026 standard premium of $202.90/month ($2,434.80 a year) and starts the one-time 6-month Medigap open enrollment period; delaying is usually the better choice, though taking it now is allowed.

This month, confirm with HR that the coverage is an active-employee group health plan (not COBRA or retiree coverage), that it stays primary after 65, and whether the plan requires enrolling in Part A or Part B at 65.

Decide on premium-free Part A (about 10 years of Medicare-taxed work, own or spouse's): it costs nothing, starts the birthday month and pays second; but if the asker or the employer contributes to an HSA, skip it, because from the first month of any Medicare the HSA contribution limit is zero (IRS Pub. 969), and Part A taken later is backdated up to 6 months (never before the month of turning 65), so HSA contributions must stop 6 months before applying.
If the asker already receives Social Security, Parts A and B are enrolled automatically: decline Part B by following SSA's instructions or contacting SSA; starting Social Security also brings Part A.

Keep the employer plan's creditable prescription drug coverage notice: Part D can also wait without penalty while that coverage continues (the Part D penalty applies only after 63 or more days without creditable coverage).

States the exception: if the job or the employer coverage ends during the 7-month Initial Enrollment Period (3 months before to 3 months after the birthday month), there is no SEP, so the asker should make sure the job and coverage last past the end of the IEP or enroll in the IEP.

At retirement: sign up about a month before employer coverage ends; with Part A already, apply for Part B online or with form CMS-40B; with Part A also deferred, apply for A and B together through SSA; either way submit CMS-L564 (Section A completed by the asker, Section B by the employer) as proof of employer coverage; enroll in Part D within 2 full months after coverage ends; Medigap open enrollment starts when Part B starts.
